chunks.text: as follow: • In Section 2, the related works and the contributions are dis- cussed. • Section 3 describes the proposed approach. • Section 4 presents the experiments, with details on the datasets and the baselines used for the comparisons. • Finally, in Section 5, conclusions are drawn and future works are outlined. 2. Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. In this section, we first provide an overview of the methods used for fruit localization and then we analyze how these methodologies are employed for yield estimation. 2.1. Object detection and counting for agriculture applications Fully supervised CNN architectures for detection and counting have achieved impressive results in a wide variety of datasets and tasks (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017; Khan et al., 2016; Bargoti and Un- derwood, 2017a). While their effectiveness is evident and extensively demonstrated, the need for massive amounts of data and supervision labels limits their practical applicability. For these reasons, weakly supervised methods have emerged as a viable and more convenient al- ternative: their objective is to guarantee performance comparable with fully-supervised baselines while relying on less informative and easier to acquire labels. A diagram depicting the fundamental difference between fully and weakly supervised methods is shown in Fig. 2(a). In the following paragraphs, we first describe fully-supervised meth- ods used for fruit detection and counting, and then we outline the weakly-supervised approaches. 2.1.1. Fully supervised methods Fruit detection and counting methods can be divided into detection- based, segmentation-based and regression-based approaches (see Fig. 2(a)). Detection-based strategies rely on CNNs that are op- timized to predict the location of fruits in the image. Counting is then achieved by simply enumerating the number of detected fruits. To perform optimization, the training images need to be annotated with ground truth bounding boxes indicating the category and the region of the image containing the object. These strategies have been successfully used in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a), Mai et al. (2020) and Mu et al. (2020). All of them rely on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) to perform detection. In particular, in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a) the model is fine-tuned to detect apples, almonds and mangoes, while in Mu et al. (2020) the authors focus on tomatoes. Instead, in Mai et al. (2020), FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) is extended to incorporate a multiple classifier fusion strategy and trained to detect oranges. Similarly, in Liu et al. (2020) the authors also consider tomatoes, however, they take advantage of the YOLO (Redmon et al., 2016) architecture. Baselines To highlight the advantages introduced by the proposed approach, we compare it against different baselines. On the ACFR-Mangoes dataset (Stein et al., 2016), the comparison is performed against the fully-supervised method proposed in Liu et al. (2019). Specifically, this approach relies on a vision-based monocular yield estimation system that is based on a FasterRCNN object detec- tor (Ren et al., 2015) coupled with a semantic structure-from-motion module. We also perform comparisons against the two versions of the method introduced by Stein et al. (2016). This yield estimation system combines a FasterRCNN object detector (Ren et al., 2015) with a LIDAR sensor to perform fruit detection and localization, while the camera pose is estimated by using a GPS/RTK system. Contributions All the weakly supervised approaches described in Section 2.1.2 are designed to regress the number of fruits in a single image. They do not provide strategies to locate and track fruits across consecutive frames. Therefore, they cannot distinguish between fruits already observed in the past or new instances, making it impossible to estimate the yield of a cultivation. On the other hand, the systems presented in Section 2.2 can track and triangulate into a global 3D map the fruits detected in the images, which allows them to estimate the total yield. However, their fruit de- tectors have some important drawbacks. Approaches such Nuske et al. (2014) and Roy and Isler (2016) employ hand-crafted features or design heuristic functions that directly process RGB image intensities, which results in systems that are very specific to the fruit species and that lack robustness to non-ideal conditions. Conversely, the strategies proposed in Stein et al. (2016), Bargoti and Underwood (2017b), Nellithimaru and Kantor (2019) and Liu et al. (2018, 2019) exploit the more robust CNN detector. However, they require full supervision to train them and, thus, do not exploit the weakly supervised paradigm. As a consequence, the data collection process for their optimization is burdensome and time-consuming, and limits their practical applicability. The approach proposed in this work aims to overcome the afore- mentioned issues. Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. In this section, we first provide an overview of the methods used for fruit localization and then we analyze how these methodologies are employed for yield estimation. 2.1. Object detection and counting for agriculture applications Fully supervised CNN architectures for detection and counting have achieved impressive results in a wide variety of datasets and tasks (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017; Khan et al., 2016; Bargoti and Un- derwood, 2017a). While their effectiveness is evident and extensively demonstrated, the need for massive amounts of data and supervision labels limits their practical applicability. For these reasons, weakly supervised methods have emerged as a viable and more convenient al- ternative: their objective is to guarantee performance comparable with fully-supervised baselines while relying on less informative and easier to acquire labels. A diagram depicting the fundamental difference between fully and weakly supervised methods is shown in Fig. 2(a). In the following paragraphs, we first describe fully-supervised meth- ods used for fruit detection and counting, and then we outline the weakly-supervised approaches. 2.1.1. Fully supervised methods Fruit detection and counting methods can be divided into detection- based, segmentation-based and regression-based approaches (see Fig. 2(a)). Detection-based strategies rely on CNNs that are op- timized to predict the location of fruits in the image. Counting is then achieved by simply enumerating the number of detected fruits. To perform optimization, the training images need to be annotated with ground truth bounding boxes indicating the category and the region of the image containing the object. These strategies have been successfully used in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a), Mai et al. (2020) and Mu et al. (2020). All of them rely on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) to perform detection. Besides the reduction of the costs, this allows extending the applicability of those systems also in indoor scenarios. Following this direction, Nellithimaru and Kantor (2019) uses only RGB images collected by a UGV for yield estimation within grape orchards. The authors take advantage of MaskRCNN (He et al., 2017) to perform fruit segmentation. Redundant counts and occlusions are avoided by localizing the robot pose and the fruit locations with a vision-based SLAM method. Multiple-counting errors can be avoided also using Structure-from-Motion, as in Liu et al. (2018, 2019). To per- form yield estimation in a mango orchard, the former uses a semantic segmentation CNN while the latter relies on an object detector one. In both cases, occlusions and redundant counts are avoided by combining a Kalman-based object tracker with a semantic Structure-from-Motion algorithm. More recently, other approaches try also to perform yield estimation with hyperspectral images, such as in Gutiérrez et al. (2019), where this sensor is used to estimate the yield in large mango orchards. 2.3. Contributions All the weakly supervised approaches described in Section 2.1.2 are designed to regress the number of fruits in a single image. They do not provide strategies to locate and track fruits across consecutive frames. Therefore, they cannot distinguish between fruits already observed in the past or new instances, making it impossible to estimate the yield of a cultivation. On the other hand, the systems presented in Section 2.2 can track and triangulate into a global 3D map the fruits detected in the images, which allows them to estimate the total yield. However, their fruit de- tectors have some important drawbacks. Approaches such Nuske et al. (2014) and Roy and Isler (2016) employ hand-crafted features or design heuristic functions that directly process RGB image intensities, which results in systems that are very specific to the fruit species and that lack robustness to non-ideal conditions. Conversely, the strategies proposed in Stein et al. (2016), Bargoti and Underwood (2017b), Nellithimaru and Kantor (2019) and Liu et al. (2018, 2019) exploit the more robust CNN detector. However, they require full supervision to train them and, thus, do not exploit the weakly supervised paradigm. As a consequence, the data collection process for their optimization is burdensome and time-consuming, and limits their practical applicability. The approach proposed in this work aims to overcome the afore- mentioned issues. In particular, it is designed to require only binary labels encoding the presence or absence of fruits in images for the training phase. Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. In this section, we first provide an overview of the methods used for fruit localization and then we analyze how these methodologies are employed for yield estimation. 2.1. Object detection and counting for agriculture applications Fully supervised CNN architectures for detection and counting have achieved impressive results in a wide variety of datasets and tasks (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017; Khan et al., 2016; Bargoti and Un- derwood, 2017a). While their effectiveness is evident and extensively demonstrated, the need for massive amounts of data and supervision labels limits their practical applicability. For these reasons, weakly supervised methods have emerged as a viable and more convenient al- ternative: their objective is to guarantee performance comparable with fully-supervised baselines while relying on less informative and easier to acquire labels. A diagram depicting the fundamental difference between fully and weakly supervised methods is shown in Fig. 2(a). In the following paragraphs, we first describe fully-supervised meth- ods used for fruit detection and counting, and then we outline the weakly-supervised approaches. 2.1.1. Fully supervised methods Fruit detection and counting methods can be divided into detection- based, segmentation-based and regression-based approaches (see Fig. 2(a)). Detection-based strategies rely on CNNs that are op- timized to predict the location of fruits in the image. Counting is then achieved by simply enumerating the number of detected fruits. To perform optimization, the training images need to be annotated with ground truth bounding boxes indicating the category and the region of the image containing the object. These strategies have been successfully used in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a), Mai et al. (2020) and Mu et al. (2020). All of them rely on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) to perform detection. In particular, in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a) the model is fine-tuned to detect apples, almonds and mangoes, while in Mu et al. (2020) the authors focus on tomatoes. Instead, in Mai et al. (2020), FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) is extended to incorporate a multiple classifier fusion strategy and trained to detect oranges. Similarly, in Liu et al. (2020) the authors also consider tomatoes, however, they take advantage of the YOLO (Redmon et al., 2016) architecture. As an alternative, CNN-based segmentation methods, which perform classification at the pixel level, could be used to measure the number 2 E. Bellocchio, F. Crocetti, G. Costante et al. On the other hand, while the labeling effort for regression methods is lower, their output does not contain information to local- ize the fruits, which is crucial to track them across frames to avoid redundant counts. 2.1.2. Weakly supervised methods Weakly supervised approaches aim to ease the burden of sample annotation by relying on less informative yet easy-to-acquire labels. Since, in this case, the optimization is not supervised with quantities that explicitly measure the desired output variable, it is common to exploit coherency losses or auxiliary tasks. An example of this process, inspired by the work presented in Bellocchio et al. (2019), is depicted in Fig. 2(b). In this case, weak supervision information ( i.e., pres- ence/absence labels) is first used to train a simple presence/absence classifier, whose goal is to predict whether the input image contains fruits or not. Its binary predictions are then combined with the counts regressed at multiple scales to impose different consistency losses and train the object count regression network. In the literature, there are several weakly supervised approaches used for object recognition, detection, semantic segmentation and in- stance segmentation (Durand et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Oquab et al., 2014; Bilen et al., 2015, 2014). Promising works that benefit from the weakly supervised paradigm have also been proposed for agricultural applications. In Marino et al. (2019) a CNN is trained with image-wise classification labels to locate several types of potato defects within the images. For fruit counting, the approach proposed in Belloc- chio et al. (2019), which we summarized in the previous paragraph and in Fig. 2(b), has been extended in Bellocchio et al. (2020), where the authors propose a quasi unsupervised framework that combines a weakly supervised counting network and an unsupervised domain adaptation method. The authors demonstrate that with this strategy it is not necessary to acquire new labels (not even weak ones) when the application domain changes (i.e., the model is used to count a fruit category different from those in the training set). Despite the interesting results achieved, most of the work previously mentioned are not specifically designed for agricultural tasks. On the other hand, those that address yield estimation ( i.e., (Bellocchio et al., 2019) and Bellocchio et al. (2020)) are not designed to locate fruits, thus, there are no straightforward ways to match them across frames and distinguish between new and already tracked elements. 2.2. Yield estimation systems The works discussed previously focus solely on the detection and counting of fruits in a single image. In this section, we summarize the approaches that integrate the counting module into a complete yield estimation system capable to track and locate fruits. These solutions mostly rely on images acquired by vision sensors mounted on a robotic platform, in some cases with the support of additional sensors such as GPS/GPS-RTK or laser and LIDAR range sensors. Estimating the yield of an entire orchard raises numerous challenges that cannot be addressed by using only the fruit detection module, in particular: • Redundant counts in sequential images: the same fruit may appear in multiple sequential frames. To avoid redundant counts of the same fruit, it is necessary to distinguish between new and old ones. • Occlusions: Fruits that are visible from a certain point of view might become occluded by foliage or other elements as the cam- era moves. Related work The importance of autonomous systems in precision farming has ex- ponentially grown in the last few years (Thayer et al., 2020; Berenstein and Edan, 2018; Williams et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020). For the yield estimation task, alongside range sensors ( e.g., LIDAR or lasers), there is increasing adoption of vision-based methods (mostly based on CNNs) that are very effective also in unstructured or partially unstructured environments. A modern vision-based yield estimation approach is a complex system capable to detect, track and map the fruits collecting streams of images. Such a system consists of different functional modules, among which the most relevant is certainly the fruit detection module. Its purpose is to detect and locate the fruits within a single image. In this section, we first provide an overview of the methods used for fruit localization and then we analyze how these methodologies are employed for yield estimation. 2.1. Object detection and counting for agriculture applications Fully supervised CNN architectures for detection and counting have achieved impressive results in a wide variety of datasets and tasks (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017; Khan et al., 2016; Bargoti and Un- derwood, 2017a). While their effectiveness is evident and extensively demonstrated, the need for massive amounts of data and supervision labels limits their practical applicability. For these reasons, weakly supervised methods have emerged as a viable and more convenient al- ternative: their objective is to guarantee performance comparable with fully-supervised baselines while relying on less informative and easier to acquire labels. A diagram depicting the fundamental difference between fully and weakly supervised methods is shown in Fig. 2(a). In the following paragraphs, we first describe fully-supervised meth- ods used for fruit detection and counting, and then we outline the weakly-supervised approaches. 2.1.1. Fully supervised methods Fruit detection and counting methods can be divided into detection- based, segmentation-based and regression-based approaches (see Fig. 2(a)). Detection-based strategies rely on CNNs that are op- timized to predict the location of fruits in the image. Counting is then achieved by simply enumerating the number of detected fruits. To perform optimization, the training images need to be annotated with ground truth bounding boxes indicating the category and the region of the image containing the object. These strategies have been successfully used in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a), Mai et al. (2020) and Mu et al. (2020). All of them rely on FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) to perform detection. In particular, in Bargoti and Underwood (2017a) the model is fine-tuned to detect apples, almonds and mangoes, while in Mu et al. (2020) the authors focus on tomatoes. Instead, in Mai et al. (2020), FasterRCNN (Ren et al., 2015) is extended to incorporate a multiple classifier fusion strategy and trained to detect oranges. Similarly, in Liu et al. (2020) the authors also consider tomatoes, however, they take advantage of the YOLO (Redmon et al., 2016) architecture. On the other hand, while the labeling effort for regression methods is lower, their output does not contain information to local- ize the fruits, which is crucial to track them across frames to avoid redundant counts. 2.1.2. Weakly supervised methods Weakly supervised approaches aim to ease the burden of sample annotation by relying on less informative yet easy-to-acquire labels. Since, in this case, the optimization is not supervised with quantities that explicitly measure the desired output variable, it is common to exploit coherency losses or auxiliary tasks. An example of this process, inspired by the work presented in Bellocchio et al. (2019), is depicted in Fig. 2(b). In this case, weak supervision information ( i.e., pres- ence/absence labels) is first used to train a simple presence/absence classifier, whose goal is to predict whether the input image contains fruits or not. Its binary predictions are then combined with the counts regressed at multiple scales to impose different consistency losses and train the object count regression network. In the literature, there are several weakly supervised approaches used for object recognition, detection, semantic segmentation and in- stance segmentation (Durand et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Oquab et al., 2014; Bilen et al., 2015, 2014). Promising works that benefit from the weakly supervised paradigm have also been proposed for agricultural applications. In Marino et al. (2019) a CNN is trained with image-wise classification labels to locate several types of potato defects within the images. For fruit counting, the approach proposed in Belloc- chio et al. (2019), which we summarized in the previous paragraph and in Fig. 2(b), has been extended in Bellocchio et al. (2020), where the authors propose a quasi unsupervised framework that combines a weakly supervised counting network and an unsupervised domain adaptation method. The authors demonstrate that with this strategy it is not necessary to acquire new labels (not even weak ones) when the application domain changes (i.e., the model is used to count a fruit category different from those in the training set). Despite the interesting results achieved, most of the work previously mentioned are not specifically designed for agricultural tasks. On the other hand, those that address yield estimation ( i.e., (Bellocchio et al., 2019) and Bellocchio et al. (2020)) are not designed to locate fruits, thus, there are no straightforward ways to match them across frames and distinguish between new and already tracked elements. 2.2.
